question:
To turn on the computer, here are the steps needed.
Step 1. Plug the power strip into the wall outlet (10 seconds)
Step 2. Connect the HDMI cable to the monitor (30 seconds)
Step 3. Toggle the master power switch on the back of the PSU (5 seconds)
Step 4. Retrieve the wireless mouse and keyboard from the drawer (45 seconds)
Step 5. Insert the CMOS battery into the motherboard (1 minute)
Step 6. Press the main chassis power button (2 seconds)
Step 7. Wait for the operating system login screen to appear (45 seconds)
Step 8. Ensure the surge protector switch is set to "On" (5 seconds)
Step 9. Allow the BIOS to complete its POST hardware check (15 seconds)
Step 10. Wait for the motherboard splash screen to display (10 seconds)
Step 11. Turn on the wireless keyboard power switch (5 seconds)
Step 12. Press the power button on the monitor bezel (3 seconds)
Step 13. Ensure the UPS backup battery is active (20 seconds)
Step 14. Check that the CPU fan begins to spin (5 seconds)
Step 15. Enter the user password to access the desktop (10 seconds)
Step 16. Connect the power cable to the back of the tower (15 seconds)
Step 17. Verify the wall socket is providing electricity (5 seconds)
Step 18. Listen for the single "System Ready" beep (2 seconds)
Step 19. Check that the internal motherboard LEDs are lit (5 seconds)
Step 20. Turn on the wireless mouse power switch (5 seconds)

These ordering constraints need to be obeyed when executing above steps:
Step 1 must precede Step 6.
Step 1 must precede Step 13.
Step 1 must precede Step 17.
Step 2 must precede Step 12.
Step 3 must precede Step 2.
Step 3 must precede Step 6.
Step 3 must precede Step 14.
Step 4 must precede Step 11.
Step 4 must precede Step 20.
Step 5 must precede Step 16.
Step 6 must precede Step 10.
Step 8 must precede Step 3.
Step 8 must precede Step 18.
Step 9 must precede Step 7.
Step 10 must precede Step 15.
Step 13 must precede Step 19.
Step 16 must precede Step 2.
Step 16 must precede Step 8.
Step 17 must precede Step 5.
Step 18 must precede Step 9.
Step 19 must precede Step 15.
Step 19 must precede Step 17.
Step 20 must precede Step 8.

Question: Assume that you need to execute all the steps to complete the task and that infinite resources are available. What is the shortest possible time to turn on the computer?

5. Use `(:durative-action ...)` with `:duration`, `:condition`, and `:effect` — not `(:action ...)`.
6. Use `(at start ...)`, `(at end ...)`, or `(over all ...)` inside `:condition` and `:effect`.
7. Initialize ALL "pending" predicates as true in the problem's `:init`.

     ```
     (:durative-action do_C :duration (= ?duration 600)
       :condition (and (at start (step_pending ?s)) (at start (a_done)))   ; ← missing (b_done)!
       :effect (and (at start (not (step_pending ?s))) (at end (step_done ?s)) (at end (c_done))))
     ```

   - GOOD (step C requires BOTH A and B — the full AND-join):

Step 1. Conduct final pre-flight systems check (2 hours)

Step 18. Conduct a static fire engine test (30 seconds)

To remove the smell of bleach from your hands, here are the steps needed.
Step 1. Locate a bottle of concentrated lemon juice (30 seconds)
Step 2. Thoroughly scrub the lemon juice into your palms and fingers (3 minutes)
Step 3. Apply a thick layer of moisturizing hand cream (2 minutes)
Step 4. Prepare a small bowl of baking soda paste (5 minutes)
Step 5. Rinse your hands under cold running water (1 minute)
Step 6. Slice a fresh orange into halves (45 seconds)
Step 7. Rub the orange peels over your skin to release citrus oils (2 minutes)
Step 8. Pour a small amount of white vinegar into a shallow dish (20 seconds)
Step 9. Rinse your hands one final time with warm water (1 minute)
Step 10. Massage the baking soda paste onto the affected areas (4 minutes)
Step 11. Wipe down the kitchen counter to clear the workspace (5 minutes)
Step 12. Locate a clean microfiber hand towel (1 minute)
Step 13. Wash your hands with mild dish soap (2 minutes)
Step 14. Pat your hands dry with the microfiber towel (30 seconds)
Step 15. Soak your fingertips in the vinegar for a deep deodorizing (5 minutes)
Step 16. Inspect your hands for any remaining bleach odor (15 seconds)
Step 17. Let the skin air dry completely (10 minutes)
Step 18. Submerge your hands in the vinegar dish (3 minutes)
Step 19. Rub a stainless steel spoon between your wet hands (90 seconds)
Step 20. Open the lemon juice bottle (10 seconds)

These ordering constraints need to be obeyed when executing above steps:

To go to college after high school, here are the steps needed.
Step 1. Research different campus cultures and locations (1 week)
Step 2. Register for the SAT or ACT exams (30 minutes)
Step 3. Pay the final tuition deposit (15 minutes)
Step 4. Request official high school transcripts (2 days)
Step 5. Purchase a study guide for entrance exams (1 hour)
Step 6. Meet with a guidance counselor to discuss goals (45 minutes)
Step 7. Draft a personal statement essay (4 days)
Step 8. Ask teachers for letters of recommendation (15 minutes)
Step 9. Attend an admitted students' campus tour (5 hours)
Step 10. Edit and polish the personal statement (2 days)
Step 11. Complete the online Common Application (3 hours)
Step 12. Sit for the standardized entrance exams (4 hours)
Step 13. Collect and upload recommendation letters (1 hour)
Step 14. Gather family financial records for FAFSA (3 hours)
Step 15. Submit the final college application and financial aid forms (1 hour)
Step 16. Receive and review admission decision letters (1 month)
Step 17. Wait for standardized test scores to be released (3 weeks)
Step 18. Write thank-you notes to recommenders (30 minutes)
Step 19. Select the college you will attend (2 weeks)
Step 20. Register for freshman orientation and dorm housing (2 hours)

These ordering constraints need to be obeyed when executing above steps:
Step 1 must precede Step 16.
Step 2 must precede Step 12.
Step 2 must precede Step 17.
Step 4 must precede Step 11.
Step 4 must precede Step 13.
Step 5 must precede Step 17.

Step 12 must precede Step 9.

Step 14 must precede Step 15.
Step 19 must precede Step 3.

To get to a job interview, here are the steps needed.
Step 1. Research the company's recent projects (2 hours)
Step 2. Print out five copies of the updated resume (10 minutes)
Step 3. Select and iron a professional outfit (30 minutes)
Step 4. Pack a briefcase with a notepad and pens (5 minutes)
Step 5. Set a backup alarm on your phone (1 minute)
Step 6. Map out the driving route and check for road closures (15 minutes)
Step 7. Put the dress shoes out by the front door (2 minutes)
Step 8. Charge your phone to full capacity (90 minutes)
Step 9. Shower and get dressed in the ironed outfit (25 minutes)
Step 10. Eat a light, energizing breakfast (20 minutes)
Step 11. Check the weather forecast (2 minutes)
Step 12. Confirm the interview time and suite number (5 minutes)
Step 13. Apply deodorant and cologne/perfume (2 minutes)
Step 14. Double-check that you have your photo ID (1 minute)
Step 15. Locate your wallet and keys (5 minutes)
Step 16. Review the interviewer's LinkedIn profile (15 minutes)
Step 17. Perform a final mirror check for stray hairs (1 minute)
Step 18. Shine your dress shoes (10 minutes)
Step 19. Drive to the office building (45 minutes)
Step 20. Brush your teeth and use mouthwash (5 minutes)

To install a new dishwasher, here are the steps needed.
Step 1. Remove the old dishwasher unit from the cavity (20 minutes)
Step 2. Slide the new dishwasher into place under the counter (10 minutes)
Step 3. Connect the water supply line to the inlet valve (15 minutes)
Step 4. Measure the height of the kitchen cabinet opening (5 minutes)
Step 5. Turn on the main water valve to check for leaks (5 minutes)
Step 6. Plug the power cord into the wall outlet (2 minutes)
Step 7. Attach the kickplate to the bottom of the machine (10 minutes)
Step 8. Dispose of the cardboard packaging (15 minutes)
Step 9. Unbox the new dishwasher in the garage (10 minutes)
Step 10. Adjust the leveling legs to match the counter height (15 minutes)
Step 11. Lay down a protective floor runner (5 minutes)
Step 12. Run a short test cycle to verify operation (30 minutes)
Step 13. Turn off the circuit breaker for the kitchen (5 minutes)
Step 14. Route the drain hose through the cabinet sidewall (10 minutes)
Step 15. Screw the mounting brackets into the underside of the counter (10 minutes)
Step 16. Remove the protective plastic film from the door (5 minutes)
Step 17. Label the breaker panel for future maintenance (2 minutes)
Step 18. Disconnect the electrical wiring from the old unit (15 minutes)
Step 19. Clear a path through the kitchen for the delivery (10 minutes)
Step 20. Break down the shipping pallet (20 minutes)

These ordering constraints need to be obeyed when executing above steps:
Step 1 must precede Step 2.

To play with your newborn, here are the steps needed.
Step 1. Place the baby on the soft play mat (30 seconds)
Step 2. Locate the box of sensory toys (2 minutes)
Step 3. Shake a colorful rattle to get their attention (1 minute)
Step 4. Hang plush animals from the activity gym bar (5 minutes)
Step 5. Select a high-contrast picture book (1 minute)
Step 6. Check that the room temperature is comfortable (30 seconds)
Step 7. Clear a safe space on the living room floor (5 minutes)
Step 8. Position a mirror at the baby's eye level (2 minutes)
Step 9. Put on some gentle background music (1 minute)
Step 10. Sanitize your hands thoroughly (45 seconds)
Step 11. Warm up a bottle for a post-play snack (8 minutes)
Step 12. Wake up from a quick power nap (20 minutes)
Step 13. Gently lay the baby down under the gym (15 seconds)
Step 14. Engage in "tummy time" exercises (10 minutes)
Step 15. Change the baby into a clean diaper (4 minutes)
Step 16. Clean the teething rings with soap (3 minutes)
Step 17. Move the coffee table out of the way (2 minutes)
Step 18. Set a timer for the next feeding (30 seconds)
Step 19. Sing a nursery rhyme while making eye contact (3 minutes)
Step 20. Dim the overhead lights (10 seconds)

To protect windows from a hurricane, here are the steps needed.
Step 1. Measure the dimensions of the window frames (30 minutes)
Step 2. Clean up the sawdust and debris from the workspace (20 minutes)
Step 3. Apply weather-stripping adhesive to the window edges (45 minutes)
Step 4. Seal the edges with waterproof silicone caulk (1 hour)
Step 5. Locate the emergency hardware kit in the garage (10 minutes)
Step 6. Purchase plywood sheets and masonry screws at the hardware store (2 hours)
Step 7. Drill pilot holes into the exterior brick facade (3 hours)
Step 8. Clear all patio furniture and plants away from the windows (1 hour)
Step 9. Mark and cut the plywood to the required sizes (90 minutes)
Step 10. Inspect the drill bits and power tools for functionality (15 minutes)
Step 11. Label each plywood board with its corresponding window location (10 minutes)
Step 12. Sand the rough edges of the cut plywood (40 minutes)
Step 13. Lift and position the heavy shutters against the frames (2 hours)
Step 14. Check the local weather radio for the storm's projected path (5 minutes)
Step 15. Coat the plywood with a quick-dry water repellent (4 hours)
Step 16. Sort the remaining mounting clips and anchors (15 minutes)
Step 17. Paint the exterior side of the boards to match the house (3 hours)
Step 18. Organize the ladder and safety harness equipment (30 minutes)
Step 19. Charge the batteries for the cordless impact driver (2 hours)

CRITICAL PDDL RULES for OPTIC planner compatibility:
1. Use ONLY `:durative-actions` and `:typing` in `:requirements`. Do NOT use `:negative-preconditions`, `:adl`, or `:disjunctive-preconditions`.
2. NEVER use `(not ...)` in action preconditions. Instead, create positive "not_done" predicates:
   - BAD:  `:condition (at start (not (task_done)))`
   - GOOD: `:condition (at start (task_pending))`

   Note: `(not ...)` is allowed in effects, just not in conditions.
3. ALL predicates must be declared in the `:predicates` block before use.
4. ALL types must be declared in the `:types` block.
5. Use `(:durative-action ...)` with `:duration`, `:condition`, and `:effect` — not `(:action ...)`.
6. Use `(at start ...)`, `(at end ...)`, or `(over all ...)` inside `:condition` and `:effect`.
7. Initialize ALL "pending" predicates as true in the problem's `:init`.

CRITICAL SEMANTIC RULES — failure to follow these causes the planner to find wrong shortcuts:
8. Every action MUST produce a UNIQUE semantic predicate (besides step_done) in its `(at end ...)` effect.
   Every action that has one or more predecessors listed in the "ordering constraints" MUST require
   ALL of those predecessors' semantic predicates as `(at start ...)` conditions — not just one of them.
   This is a DAG (not a linear chain): a step may have multiple direct predecessors and ALL must be
   enforced, otherwise the planner can skip slow predecessors and find an illegally short makespan.
   - BAD (step C requires only A but not B, so planner skips slow B):
     ```
     (:durative-action do_A :duration (= ?duration 3600)
       :condition (at start (step_pending ?s))
       :effect (and (at start (not (step_pending ?s))) (at end (step_done ?s)) (at end (a_done))))
     (:durative-action do_B :duration (= ?duration 7200)
       :condition (at start (step_pending ?s))
       :effect (and (at start (not (step_pending ?s))) (at end (step_done ?s)) (at end (b_done))))
     (:durative-action do_C :duration (= ?duration 600)
       :condition (and (at start (step_pending ?s)) (at start (a_done)))   ; ← missing (b_done)!
       :effect (and (at start (not (step_pending ?s))) (at end (step_done ?s)) (at end (c_done))))
     ```
   - GOOD (step C requires BOTH A and B — the full AND-join):
     ```
     (:durative-action do_A :duration (= ?duration 3600)
       :condition (at start (step_pending ?s))
       :effect (and (at start (not (step_pending ?s))) (at end (step_done ?s)) (at end (a_done))))
     (:durative-action do_B :duration (= ?duration 7200)
       :condition (at start (step_pending ?s))
       :effect (and (at start (not (step_pending ?s))) (at end (step_done ?s)) (at end (b_done))))
     (:durative-action do_C :duration (= ?duration 600)
       :condition (and (at start (step_pending ?s)) (at start (a_done)) (at start (b_done)))   ; ← both
       :effect (and (at start (not (step_pending ?s))) (at end (step_done ?s)) (at end (c_done))))
     ```

   Steps with NO predecessors listed in the constraints need only `(at start (step_pending ?s))`.

2. NEVER use `(not ...)` in action preconditions. Instead, create positive "not_done" predicates:

   Note: `(not ...)` is allowed in effects, just not in conditions.
3. ALL predicates must be declared in the `:predicates` block before use.
4. ALL types must be declared in the `:types` block.
5. Use `(:durative-action ...)` with `:duration`, `:condition`, and `:effect` — not `(:action ...)`.
6. Use `(at start ...)`, `(at end ...)`, or `(over all ...)` inside `:condition` and `:effect`.
7. Initialize ALL "pending" predicates as true in the problem's `:init`.

CRITICAL SEMANTIC RULES — failure to follow these causes the planner to find wrong shortcuts:
8. Every action MUST produce a UNIQUE semantic predicate (besides step_done) in its `(at end ...)` effect.
   Every action that has one or more predecessors listed in the "ordering constraints" MUST require
   ALL of those predecessors' semantic predicates as `(at start ...)` conditions — not just one of them.
   This is a DAG (not a linear chain): a step may have multiple direct predecessors and ALL must be
   enforced, otherwise the planner can skip slow predecessors and find an illegally short makespan.
   - BAD (step C requires only A but not B, so planner skips slow B):
     ```
     (:durative-action do_A :duration (= ?duration 3600)
       :condition (at start (step_pending ?s))

       :effect (and (at start (not (step_pending ?s))) (at end (step_done ?s)) (at end (b_done))))
     (:durative-action do_C :duration (= ?duration 600)
       :condition (and (at start (step_pending ?s)) (at start (a_done)))   ; ← missing (b_done)!
       :effect (and (at start (not (step_pending ?s))) (at end (step_done ?s)) (at end (c_done))))
     ```
   - GOOD (step C requires BOTH A and B — the full AND-join):
     ```
     (:durative-action do_A :duration (= ?duration 3600)
       :condition (at start (step_pending ?s))
       :effect (and (at start (not (step_pending ?s))) (at end (step_done ?s)) (at end (a_done))))
     (:durative-action do_B :duration (= ?duration 7200)
       :condition (at start (step_pending ?s))
     ```

CRITICAL PDDL RULES for OPTIC planner compatibility:

   - BAD:  `:condition (at start (not (task_done)))`
   - GOOD: `:condition (at start (task_pending))`

   Note: `(not ...)` is allowed in effects, just not in conditions.
3. ALL predicates must be declared in the `:predicates` block before use.
4. ALL types must be declared in the `:types` block.
5. Use `(:durative-action ...)` with `:duration`, `:condition`, and `:effect` — not `(:action ...)`.
6. Use `(at start ...)`, `(at end ...)`, or `(over all ...)` inside `:condition` and `:effect`.
7. Initialize ALL "pending" predicates as true in the problem's `:init`.

CRITICAL SEMANTIC RULES — failure to follow these causes the planner to find wrong shortcuts:
8. Every action MUST produce a UNIQUE semantic predicate (besides step_done) in its `(at end ...)` effect.
   Every action that has one or more predecessors listed in the "ordering constraints" MUST require
   ALL of those predecessors' semantic predicates as `(at start ...)` conditions — not just one of them.
   This is a DAG (not a linear chain): a step may have multiple direct predecessors and ALL must be
   enforced, otherwise the planner can skip slow predecessors and find an illegally short makespan.
   - BAD (step C requires only A but not B, so planner skips slow B):
     ```
     (:durative-action do_A :duration (= ?duration 3600)
       :condition (at start (step_pending ?s))
       :effect (and (at start (not (step_pending ?s))) (at end (step_done ?s)) (at end (a_done))))

       :effect (and (at start (not (step_pending ?s))) (at end (step_done ?s)) (at end (b_done))))

       :condition (and (at start (step_pending ?s)) (at start (a_done)))   ; ← missing (b_done)!
       :effect (and (at start (not (step_pending ?s))) (at end (step_done ?s)) (at end (c_done))))
     ```
   - GOOD (step C requires BOTH A and B — the full AND-join):
     ```
     (:durative-action do_A :duration (= ?duration 3600)
       :condition (at start (step_pending ?s))
       :effect (and (at start (not (step_pending ?s))) (at end (step_done ?s)) (at end (a_done))))
     (:durative-action do_B :duration (= ?duration 7200)
       :condition (at start (step_pending ?s))
       :effect (and (at start (not (step_pending ?s))) (at end (step_done ?s)) (at end (b_done))))

       :effect (and (at start (not (step_pending ?s))) (at end (step_done ?s)) (at end (c_done))))
     ```

To learn how to play the violin, here are the steps needed.
Step 1. Perform a simple folk song for family (5 minutes)
Step 2. Memorize the finger patterns for the G Major scale (2 hours)
Step 3. Learn how to read basic sheet music notation (3 days)
Step 4. Practice transitioning between the D and A strings (4 hours)
Step 5. Attend a formal introductory recital (1 hour)
Step 6. Purchase a beginner-grade violin and bow (2 hours)
Step 7. Research local violin instructors (3 hours)
Step 8. Apply rosin to the bow hair for the first time (2 minutes)
Step 9. Tighten the bow hair and tune the strings (10 minutes)
Step 10. Master the "Twinkle Twinkle Little Star" variations (1 week)
Step 11. Buy a sturdy music stand (15 minutes)
Step 12. Sign up for an advanced masterclass (30 minutes)
Step 13. Watch an online tutorial on bow maintenance (20 minutes)
Step 14. Record a video of your progress for self-critique (10 minutes)
Step 15. Set up a dedicated practice space in the house (1 hour)
Step 16. Rent a shoulder rest for better ergonomics (20 minutes)
Step 17. Learn the proper way to hold the violin and bow (45 minutes)
Step 18. Practice bowing straight across the strings (5 hours)
Step 19. Complete a week of daily open-string exercises (7 days)
Step 20. Participate in the advanced masterclass session (2 hours)

These ordering constraints need to be obeyed when executing above steps:
Step 2 must precede Step 10.

Step 2. Complete a 20-mile long distance training run (4 hours)

Step 11. Create a high-energy playlist for motivation (45 minutes)
Step 12. Buy a GPS running watch to track pace (20 minutes)
Step 13. Increase carbohydrate intake for energy loading (3 days)
Step 14. Read the official marathon rulebook (40 minutes)
Step 15. Run the actual 26.2 mile marathon course (5 hours)
Step 16. Pick up your race bib and timing chip at the expo (2 hours)
Step 17. Download a 16-week marathon training plan (10 minutes)
Step 18. Volunteer at a water station for a smaller race (4 hours)
Step 19. Drive to the starting line on race morning (45 minutes)
Step 20. Execute the 16-week training schedule (4 months)

CRITICAL PDDL RULES for OPTIC planner compatibility:
1. Use ONLY `:durative-actions` and `:typing` in `:requirements`. Do NOT use `:negative-preconditions`, `:adl`, or `:disjunctive-preconditions`.
2. NEVER use `(not ...)` in action preconditions. Instead, create positive "not_done" predicates:
   - BAD:  `:condition (at start (not (task_done)))`
   - GOOD: `:condition (at start (task_pending))`
   Then in `:effect`, set `(not (task_pending))` and `(task_done)`.
   Note: `(not ...)` is allowed in effects, just not in conditions.
3. ALL predicates must be declared in the `:predicates` block before use.
4. ALL types must be declared in the `:types` block.
5. Use `(:durative-action ...)` with `:duration`, `:condition`, and `:effect` — not `(:action ...)`.
6. Use `(at start ...)`, `(at end ...)`, or `(over all ...)` inside `:condition` and `:effect`.
7. Initialize ALL "pending" predicates as true in the problem's `:init`.

CRITICAL SEMANTIC RULES — failure to follow these causes the planner to find wrong shortcuts:
8. Every action MUST produce a UNIQUE semantic predicate (besides step_done) in its `(at end ...)` effect.
   Every action that has one or more predecessors listed in the "ordering constraints" MUST require
   ALL of those predecessors' semantic predicates as `(at start ...)` conditions — not just one of them.
   This is a DAG (not a linear chain): a step may have multiple direct predecessors and ALL must be
   enforced, otherwise the planner can skip slow predecessors and find an illegally short makespan.
   - BAD (step C requires only A but not B, so planner skips slow B):
     ```
     (:durative-action do_A :duration (= ?duration 3600)
       :condition (at start (step_pending ?s))
       :effect (and (at start (not (step_pending ?s))) (at end (step_done ?s)) (at end (a_done))))
     (:durative-action do_B :duration (= ?duration 7200)
       :condition (at start (step_pending ?s))
       :effect (and (at start (not (step_pending ?s))) (at end (step_done ?s)) (at end (b_done))))
     (:durative-action do_C :duration (= ?duration 600)
       :condition (and (at start (step_pending ?s)) (at start (a_done)))   ; ← missing (b_done)!
       :effect (and (at start (not (step_pending ?s))) (at end (step_done ?s)) (at end (c_done))))
     ```
   - GOOD (step C requires BOTH A and B — the full AND-join):
     ```
     (:durative-action do_A :duration (= ?duration 3600)
       :condition (at start (step_pending ?s))
       :effect (and (at start (not (step_pending ?s))) (at end (step_done ?s)) (at end (a_done))))
     (:durative-action do_B :duration (= ?duration 7200)
       :condition (at start (step_pending ?s))
       :effect (and (at start (not (step_pending ?s))) (at end (step_done ?s)) (at end (b_done))))
     (:durative-action do_C :duration (= ?duration 600)
       :condition (and (at start (step_pending ?s)) (at start (a_done)) (at start (b_done)))   ; ← both
       :effect (and (at start (not (step_pending ?s))) (at end (step_done ?s)) (at end (c_done))))
     ```
   Steps with NO predecessors listed in the constraints need only `(at start (step_pending ?s))`.
9. The problem's `:goal` MUST include the FINAL semantic predicate (the outcome of the last action in the chain),
   in addition to all `(step_done stepN)` conditions.
   - BAD (planner completes all steps trivially using only the fastest action):
     ```
     (:goal (and (step_done step1) (step_done step2) ... (step_done step6)))
     ```
   - GOOD (forces the planner to execute the full causal chain):
     ```
     (:goal (and (step_done step1) (step_done step2) ... (step_done step6) (departure_prepared)))
     ```
10. Every action's `:duration` MUST come from the time stated in the problem for that step.
    NEVER give any action a duration of 1 second (or any tiny placeholder) unless the problem
    explicitly states that step takes 1 second.
    Do NOT split a step into "the real work" + a 1-second "state confirmation" action —
    the semantic predicate is simply an effect of the step's action, not a separate action.
    - BAD (the act of "buying beer" is given 1 second; its real duration is absorbed into prior steps):
      ```
      (:durative-action give_money      :duration (= ?duration 120) :effect (at end (money_given)))
      (:durative-action buy_beer        :duration (= ?duration 1)   :effect (at end (beer_bought)))
      ; "buy_beer" should have the duration from the problem, not 1 second
      ```
    - GOOD (each step uses the duration stated in the problem):
      ```
      (:durative-action give_money      :duration (= ?duration 120) :effect (at end (money_given)))
      (:durative-action buy_beer        :duration (= ?duration 60)  ; ← from the problem statement
        :effect (and (at end (step_done ?s)) (at end (beer_bought))))
      ```
11. A `:durative-action` may only have ONE `:condition` keyword. If multiple conditions are needed,
    wrap them ALL in a single `(and ...)` block. Never write multiple separate `:condition` lines.
    - BAD (PDDL parsers only keep the last `:condition`, silently dropping all others):
      ```
      :condition (at start (supplies_obtained))
      :condition (at start (step_pending ?s))
      ```
    - GOOD:
      ```
      :condition (and (at start (supplies_obtained)) (at start (step_pending ?s)))
      ```
12. The number of `:durative-actions` MUST exactly equal the number of steps (one action per step).
    Declare exactly N step objects (step1 ... stepN) for N steps. Never generate more or fewer actions
    than steps — extra actions let the planner skip the most expensive one.
    - BAD (7 actions but only 6 step objects — planner skips the slowest action):
      ```
      (:objects step1 step2 step3 step4 step5 step6 - step)
      ; but domain defines 7 durative-actions including an expensive assemble_X (1200s)
      ; planner uses the 6 cheapest actions and ignores assemble_X entirely
      ```
    - GOOD:
      ```
      (:objects step1 step2 step3 step4 step5 step6 step7 - step)  ; 7 steps → 7 actions
      ```

To have for dinner, here are the steps needed.
Step 1. Chop the onions and garlic (10 minutes)
Step 2. Simmer the tomato sauce (45 minutes)
Step 3. Open the canned tomatoes (2 minutes)
Step 4. Thaw the frozen ground beef (2 hours)
Step 5. Wash the fresh basil (5 minutes)
Step 6. Set the dining table (5 minutes)
Step 7. Finely mince the basil leaves (5 minutes)
Step 8. Sauté the vegetables in olive oil (8 minutes)
Step 9. Combine all ingredients into the final stew (15 minutes)
Step 10. Retrieve ingredients from the pantry (5 minutes)
Step 11. Boil a large pot of water (12 minutes)
Step 12. Grate the parmesan cheese (3 minutes)
Step 13. Sharpen the kitchen knife (4 minutes)
Step 14. Preheat the heavy Dutch oven (10 minutes)
Step 15. Locate the cheese grater (1 minute)
Step 16. Iron the linen napkins (15 minutes)
Step 17. Prepare the workstation for cooking (5 minutes)
Step 18. Clean the kitchen counter (10 minutes)
Step 19. Reduce the sauce to a thick consistency (20 minutes)
Step 20. Measure out the dried spices (3 minutes)

These ordering constraints need to be obeyed when executing above steps:
Step 1 must precede Step 8.
Step 1 must precede Step 9.
Step 2 must precede Step 19.
Step 3 must precede Step 2.
Step 3 must precede Step 20.
Step 4 must precede Step 9.
Step 4 must precede Step 17.
Step 5 must precede Step 7.
Step 7 must precede Step 2.
Step 10 must precede Step 5.
Step 10 must precede Step 8.
Step 11 must precede Step 17.
Step 13 must precede Step 1.
Step 14 must precede Step 9.
Step 15 must precede Step 12.
Step 16 must precede Step 6.
Step 16 must precede Step 18.
Step 17 must precede Step 13.
Step 18 must precede Step 17.
Step 19 must precede Step 9.
Step 20 must precede Step 17.
